# Voice profile — eff-mullin

## 1. Cadence

Sentences run at medium length while building an argument, then snap short to land the consequence. After one or two sentences of explanation or qualification, a third delivers the point in eight words or fewer — 9/11 samples, several times per piece (`why-are-gay-bars`: *"This was not simply checking IDs at the door. PatronScan was building a database."*; `kids-online-safety`: *"When the safest legal option is to delete a forum, platforms will delete the forum."*). If you have let a sentence run, make the next one short and flat.

Interruption punctuation is heavy and carries two distinct loads. Parentheses run throughout all 11 samples — 97 instances, 12.03 per 1,000 words ([measurement:round-parenthetical-spans] each non-nested pair of round brackets whose contents stay on one line) — used for brief definitions, background, and citations that would stall a clause if written out. Em-dashes run through 10/11 samples — 53 instances, 6.57 per 1,000 words ([measurement:em-dashes] every literal em-dash character) — used for emphasis and abrupt elaboration. Their combined rate is roughly 18 per 1,000 words; use both, and use them often.

## 2. How a piece opens

Nine of eleven pieces name the legislation or primary controversy in the first sentence — 9/11 (`kids-online-safety`: *"The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA) is back in the Senate."*; `congress-just-rushed`: *"In a voice vote earlier this week, the House of Representatives passed H.R. 6028, the 'Legislative Branch Agencies Clarification Act.'"*). The opening sentence is declarative and often embeds a characterization in the verb: the bill "would fundamentally change," "is supposed to target," "still demands."

Five of those pieces follow the opening with a concession-and-pivot — 5/11, once per piece: a sentence acknowledging what the bill claims to do, immediately followed by "But" or "In reality" (`californias-ab-412-bill`: *"At first glance, this might sound like a reasonable step toward transparency. But it's an impossible standard..."*; `no-fakes`: *"The NO FAKES Act is supposed to target harmful AI-generated impersonations. But in reality, it will make it easier to suppress commentary, satire, and other lawful speech."*). Name the bill, concede its stated aim, pivot.

## 3. How a piece closes

Eight of eleven samples end on a declarative statement of principle, a direct call to action, or both — 8/11 (`congress-rushed`: *"The Copyright Office should serve the public—not presidential administrations, and not industry lobbyists."*; `kids-online-safety`: *"Lawmakers should reject it, and fast."*). The closing sentence is short. Close by naming who should do what, or by naming a value the piece has been building toward. Do not qualify the close.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The dominant first person is institutional. The pieces speak as EFF: "we" at 19 instances, 2.36 per 1,000 words ([measurement:first-person-plural-family] case-sensitive whole-word tokens we, We, us, our, Our, ours, Ours, and the listed contracted we forms; uppercase US excluded), 10/11 samples. The authorial "I" is near-absent: 2 instances total, 0.25 per 1,000 words ([measurement:first-person-singular-family] case-insensitive whole-word I, me, my, mine, myself), 2/11 samples. Write "EFF" or "we," not "I."

Contractions run throughout — 86 instances, 10.66 per 1,000 words ([measurement:contractions] whole-word n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, and 'm forms, plus 's for the closed elision hosts enumerated in the measurement only; possessive 's excluded), all 11 samples. Uncontracted negatives (do not, cannot, should not, and the full list of phrases — [measurement:uncontracted-negatives] case-insensitive whole phrases including does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, could not, would not, will not, have not, has not, had not) appear at 32 instances, 3.97 per 1,000 words, 9/11 samples. The ratio is roughly 2.7 contractions per uncontracted negative; the register is conversational despite formal subject matter. Hit the contraction rate, not the uncontracted rate.

Second person is sparse — 11 instances, 1.36 per 1,000 words ([measurement:second-person-family] case-insensitive whole-word you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, you'll), 5/11 samples. When it appears, it addresses a reader being asked to act or placed in a hypothetical scenario. It does not carry the argument.

Question marks are rare — 9 instances, 1.12 per 1,000 words ([measurement:question-marks] every literal question-mark character), 4/11 samples. Questions set up the paragraph that answers them; most pieces have none. One or two per piece at most.

Uncertainty and prediction are carried by modal verbs — "may," "might," "will likely," "could be read" — 8/11 samples, several times per piece. No hedging phrases like "I think" or "I believe" appear. No rate: I cannot enumerate modal instances under a counting rule that separates predictive from deontic or epistemic uses in a reproducible way.

## 5. Figures

Figures are brief, idiomatic, and drawn from legal, political, and crime vocabulary — 8/11 samples, several times per piece. They do not extend beyond a phrase. The vocabulary across the corpus: *death sentence*, *cumbersome beast*, *jumping the gun*, *smokescreen*, *dragnet*, *legislative sleight-of-hand*, *heckler's veto*, *gift to Big Tech* (`californias-ab-412-bill`, `kids-online-safety`, `no-fakes`). No figure comes from nature, the body, or abstract philosophy. I cannot bound "a figure" for counting purposes; this is the vocabulary the figures are built from — use it at roughly one or two idiomatic phrases per 500 words.

## 6. Register range

The register does not shift across pieces; differences are structural. Longer pieces are divided by bold subheadings — 9/11 samples; the two without subheadings (`court-records`, `no-fakes`) are both under 400 words. Headings tend to be declarative sentences or noun phrases that carry the argument rather than label it neutrally: *"This Bill Was Rushed Through," "A Burden That Can't Be Met," "Courts Are Already Deciding These Questions."*

Opponents are named structurally — 8/11 samples, several times per piece: "Big Tech," "large content companies," "copyright trolls," "the largest corporations." Named individuals are rare. The argument is carried by the institutional voice alone; allies and co-signatories are named by reference link, not quoted at length as the spine of a point.

## 7. What the corpus never does

The pieces carry no personal authorial presence. Against 2 first-person singular instances at 0.25 per 1,000 words ([measurement:first-person-singular-family]), there are 19 first-person plural instances at 2.36 per 1,000 words ([measurement:first-person-plural-family]). The institutional "we" occupies the space the personal "I" would otherwise fill. No personal anecdote, biographical detail, or first-hand account from the author as a person appears in any of the 11 samples. Write in the institutional voice throughout; the absence count (2 singular instances, 0.25 per 1,000 words) should stay at or below that rate.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

`voice.md` was empty; all observations derive from the corpus alone.

**Register toward a supportive outcome.** All 11 samples oppose or critique legislation. The corpus does not show how this voice behaves when writing in support of a bill or celebrating a win. The concession-pivot opening and declarative imperative close may be specific to the opposition-piece format.

**Modal hedging rate.** Predictive modals run through 8/11 samples and are real, but no reproducible counting rule separates predictive from deontic or epistemic uses. The observation is qualitative only.

**Profanity pairing.** Profanity is 0 instances across all 11 samples ([measurement:profanity-vulgarity]). The format requires an enumerable positive complement; the complementary positive—the institutional formal vocabulary that occupies this space—is not independently enumerable as a rate. The instruction is: use no profanity.

**Typographic versus authorial origin.** Em-dashes (53 instances, 10/11 samples) and parentheses (97 instances, 11/11 samples) are treated as authorial for a CC-BY-4.0 web publication where compositor intervention is unlikely. En-dashes are nearly absent (7 instances, 0.87 per 1,000 words, 1/11 samples); whether this asymmetry reflects authorial preference or platform rendering is not determinable from the corpus.

**Observations dropped:** 3 — subheading form distinction (declarative versus noun-phrase, pattern too mixed to claim), en-dash as authorial style (typographic uncertainty), tricolon sentence-endings (2–3 clear examples across 11 samples, below the two-sample citation floor for a stated habit).
